TTL Cache — Cache with Expiry

Each entry has a time-to-live. After TTL expires, the entry is invalid. Uses lazy expiration on get() — no background scanner needed for the basic version. Generic <K, V> with per-key TTL overrides.
Medium-Hard Amazon · Google · Microsoft Generic <K, V>
get() O(1) put() O(1) cleanup() O(n)

Core Idea

What is a TTL Cache?

A key-value store where each entry has an absolute expiry time. Reads check if the entry is still alive; expired entries are treated as cache misses.

Think Redis SETEX / EXPIRE — the same concept.

Two Expiration Strategies

LazyActive
WhenOn get()Background scan
CostO(1) per callO(n) per sweep
MemoryStale entries lingerCleaned promptly
Used byRedis uses both: lazy + probabilistic sweep

Operations

put(key, val)

  1. Compute expiryTime = now + ttlMs
  2. Store Entry(value, expiryTime) in HashMap

get(key)

  1. Look up Entry in HashMap
  2. If null → return null
  3. If isExpired() → remove + return null
  4. Else → return value

cleanup()

  1. Iterate all entries
  2. Remove expired ones
  3. O(n) — for periodic use
1

Entry — stores value + expiry

inner class
private static class Entry<V> {
    V value;
    long expiryTime; // absolute time when entry expires

    Entry(V value, long expiryTime) {
        this.value = value;
        this.expiryTime = expiryTime;
    }
    boolean isExpired() {
        return System.currentTimeMillis() > expiryTime;
    }
}
2

Fields & Constructor

private final Map<K, Entry<V>> map = new HashMap<>();
private final long defaultTtlMs;

public TTLCache(long defaultTtlMs) {
    this.defaultTtlMs = defaultTtlMs;
}
3

put() — with optional per-key TTL

public void put(K key, V value) {
    put(key, value, defaultTtlMs);
}

public void put(K key, V value, long ttlMs) {
    map.put(key, new Entry<>(value, System.currentTimeMillis() + ttlMs));
}
4

get() — lazy expiration

public V get(K key) {
    Entry<V> entry = map.get(key);
    if (entry == null) return null;
    if (entry.isExpired()) {
        map.remove(key);  // lazy expiration
        return null;
    }
    return entry.value;
}
5

Helpers — containsKey, size, cleanup

public boolean containsKey(K key) { return get(key) != null; }

public int size() { cleanup(); return map.size(); }

// Active cleanup — remove all expired entries
private void cleanup() {
    map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue().isExpired());
}

Common Follow-ups

How does Redis handle expiry?

Both lazy + active. Lazy: check on every read. Active: probabilistic — every 100ms, sample 20 random keys, delete expired ones. If > 25% were expired, repeat immediately. This keeps expired key % below ~25% without full scans.

TTL + LRU combined?

Store expiryTime in each LRU Node. On get(), first check if expired (treat as miss + evict). On put(), set expiry. Combine this file's TTL logic with the LRU Cache's linked list structure.

Efficient cleanup with a priority queue?

Use a PriorityQueue<Entry> ordered by expiryTime. On cleanup, keep polling while peek().isExpired(). This avoids scanning non-expired entries — only process the ones that are actually due. Cost: O(k log n) where k = number expired.

Thread-safe TTL cache?

Use ConcurrentHashMap for the map + a ScheduledExecutorService for periodic cleanup. Or use Caffeine / Guava Cache in production — they handle TTL, LRU, and concurrency out of the box.

3

Edge Cases & Gotchas

Clock skew — System.currentTimeMillis() can jump backward (NTP sync). For short TTLs, use System.nanoTime() which is monotonic. For distributed systems, use logical clocks.
Memory leak with lazy-only — If keys are written but never read again, expired entries accumulate. Must have periodic cleanup for production use.
Per-key TTL — The overloaded put(key, value, ttlMs) allows different TTLs per entry. This is how Redis SETEX works — global default + per-key override.
